collection: NECO BECE History JSS 3 original conceptual practice
note: Original objective practice with provisional historical topic mapping and four-option classroom format. Current NECO objectives and curriculum adoption remain unverified. Source errors are recorded in the registry.

questions.subject: History
questions.learningObjective: Recognise administration through existing local authorities.
questions.prompt: In a classroom description of colonial administration, an official gives instructions through an existing local ruler, who carries them out under colonial supervision. Which system is being illustrated?
options: Indirect rule.
Complete political independence.
A government without local authorities.
An elected national republic.
questions.explanation: Indirect rule used local authorities within a system controlled by the colonial administration.

questions.subject: History
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish commercial contact from other forms of contact.
questions.prompt: Which activity is the clearest example of commercial contact between British visitors and Nigerian communities?
options: A missionary teaching a religious lesson.
Merchants negotiating purchases of local produce.
An explorer recording the course of a river.
A teacher explaining a map in class.
questions.answer: Merchants negotiating purchases of local produce.
questions.explanation: Purchasing produce is a trading activity. The other activities have different immediate purposes.

questions.subject: History
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish military conquest from voluntary political agreement.
questions.prompt: A learner says that a territory brought under colonial control after military defeat must have freely chosen the new government. Which response best evaluates the claim?
options: Military defeat always proves popular approval.
Colonial control could occur only after an election.
Control gained through force does not establish free consent.
The use of force makes historical evidence unnecessary.
questions.answer: Control gained through force does not establish free consent.
questions.explanation: Military defeat can impose control. It does not demonstrate that the population freely agreed.

questions.subject: History
questions.learningObjective: Explain amalgamation as an administrative joining rather than independence.
questions.prompt: Which description best explains amalgamation in the historical development of Nigeria?
options: The immediate end of all British colonial authority.
The replacement of every local language by one language.
The disappearance of all differences among communities.
The joining of previously separate colonial administrations.
questions.answer: The joining of previously separate colonial administrations.
questions.explanation: Amalgamation joined administrations. It did not itself end colonial rule or erase social differences.

questions.subject: History
questions.learningObjective: Identify the political aim of anti-colonial nationalism.
questions.prompt: A study group examines demands for Nigerians to have greater control over their own government. In the independence movement, these demands are best associated with which aim?
options: Self-government and an end to colonial domination.
Permanent exclusion of Nigerians from public decisions.
The extension of overseas rule without local participation.
The ending of all communication between communities.
questions.answer: Self-government and an end to colonial domination.
questions.explanation: Anti-colonial nationalism sought political control and self-government rather than continued external domination.

questions.subject: History
questions.learningObjective: Recognise independence movements as involving multiple participants.
questions.prompt: Why would an account of Nigeria’s independence movement be incomplete if it discussed only one prominent leader?
options: Only one person could take part in political activity.
The movement involved several leaders, organisations and supporters.
The identity of every participant is irrelevant to History.
All participants always used identical methods.
questions.answer: The movement involved several leaders, organisations and supporters.
questions.explanation: A broad movement includes multiple contributors. Studying only one person can hide their roles and differing approaches.
